Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: Genetically determined 25(OH)D was not causally associated with depression in Mendelian randomization analysis.
Sentence: "Although a selection of nine outcomes were reported in previous Mendelian-randomization studies or umbrella reviews to be associated with vitamin D, our MR analysis, with substantial study power (>80% power to detect an association with an odds ratio >1.2 for per standard deviation increase of log-transformed 25[OH]D), was unable to support an interpretation of causal association."
Measured as: depression
Population: 339,256 individuals of White British origin from UK Biobank
Intervention: Genetically determined 25(OH)D level (polygenic risk score, Mendelian randomization)
Comparator: Lower genetically determined 25(OH)D levels
Design: other primary study
Sample size: 339,256
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Among women supplemented with 800 IU vitamin D, those who remained vitamin D deficient before delivery had a significantly higher incidence of depression than those who reached insufficiency.
Sentence: "The incidence of depression in patients in vitamin D deficiency group following vitamin D supplementation was significantly higher than insufficiency group and reached statistical significance (P < 0.001)."
Measured as: incidence of prenatal depression
Population: Pregnant women diagnosed with vitamin D deficiency at 12-14 weeks of gestation, single tertiary hospital in Chengdu, China
Intervention: Vitamin D 800 IU daily from 14 weeks of gestation
Comparator: Women who achieved vitamin D insufficiency after supplementation versus those who remained deficient
Design: cohort study
Sample size: 1,365
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

## Responses
